extracted.intended_audience: chemical manufacturers, importers, distributors, employers, and occupational safety/health professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory criteria for preparing, providing, storing, and using Safety Data Sheets (SDS) and for classifying health hazards of substances and mixtures under OSHA's revised hazard communication aligned with the GHS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required SDS sections and ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: An SDS must include at least the following section numbers and headings, and associated information under each heading, in the order listed: (i) Section 1, Identification; (ii) Section 2, Hazard(s) identification; (iii) Section 3, Composition/information on ingredients; (iv) Section 4, First-aid measures; (v) Section 5, Fire-fighting measures; (vi) Section 6, Accidental release measures; (vii) Section 7, Handling and storage; (viii) Section 8, Exposure controls/personal protection; (ix) Section 9, Physical and chemical properties; (x) Section 10, Stability and reactivity; (xi) Section 11, Toxicological information; (xii) Section 12, Ecological information; (xiii) Section 13, Disposal considerations; (xiv) Section 14, Transport information; (xv) Section 15, Regulatory information; and (xvi) Section 16, Other information, including date of preparation or last revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: To be consistent with the GHS, an SDS must also include the headings in paragraphs (g)(2)(xii) through (g)(2)(xv) in order. OSHA will not be enforcing information requirements in sections 12 through 15, as these areas are not under its jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributor obligations for providing SDSs
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributors shall ensure safety data sheets, and updated information, are provided to other distributors and employers with their initial shipment and with the first shipment after an SDS is updated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (i) Provide SDSs with shipped containers or send prior to/at time of shipment; (ii) Retail distributors selling to employers with commercial accounts must provide an SDS upon request and post signage that an SDS is available; (iii) Wholesale distributors selling over-the-counter shall provide SDSs upon employer request and post signage; (iv) If employer without commercial account purchases from retail distributor not required to have SDSs on file, the retail distributor must provide manufacturer/importer/distributor contact info upon request; (v) Wholesale distributors must provide SDSs to employers or other distributors upon request; (vi) Manufacturers/importers/distributors need not provide SDSs to retail distributors that inform them they do not sell to commercial accounts or open sealed containers for use in their own workplaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: SDS storage and accessibility requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Safety data sheets may be kept in any form, including as operating procedures, and may be stored to cover groups of hazardous chemicals in a work area where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employer must ensure the required information is provided for each hazardous chemical and is readily accessible during each work shift to employees when they are in their work area(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade secret claims for specific chemical identity and concentrations (SDS Section 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chemical manufacturers, importers, or employers may withhold specific chemical identity and/or the exact percentage or concentration range of a substance in a mixture from section 3 of the SDS if the trade secret claim can be supported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions: (i) Claim supported; (ii) SDS still discloses properties and effects; (iii) SDS indicates that identity/concentration is withheld as trade secret; (iv) If concentration withheld, provide the ingredient's concentration as one of prescribed ranges (A–M, e.g., 0.1%–1%, 0.5%–1.5%, ... up to 80%–100%); (v) Prescribed range used must be the narrowest possible; (vi) Manufacturers may provide a narrower range than prescribed; (vii) Specific identity and exact concentration/range must be made available to health professionals, employees, and designated representatives in accordance with paragraph (i).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade secret disclosure to treating health professionals in emergencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a treating PLHCP determines that a medical emergency exists and the specific chemical identity and/or specific concentration or concentration range is necessary for emergency or first-aid treatment, the chemical manufacturer, importer, or employer shall immediately disclose that information to the treating PLHCP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure is required immediately regardless of written statements or confidentiality agreements; the manufacturer/importer/employer may require a written statement of need and confidentiality agreement as soon as circumstances permit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade secret disclosure in non-emergency situations
rubrics_metrics.description: In non-emergency situations, a manufacturer/importer/employer shall, upon request, disclose a specific chemical identity or exact concentration/range otherwise permitted to be withheld as a trade secret to a health professional, employee, or designated representative if specified conditions are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request requirements: (i) must be in writing; (ii) must describe with reasonable detail one or more occupational health needs (assess hazards, conduct sampling, medical surveillance, provide medical treatment, select PPE, design controls, conduct health-effects studies); (iii) explain why available disclosed information would not satisfy the purpose; (iv) include procedures to maintain confidentiality; (v) the health professional and requester must agree in a written confidentiality agreement limiting use and release and permitting OSHA access as provided. See specific paragraph references for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective and compliance dates and transition allowances
rubrics_metrics.description: This section becomes effective July 19, 2024, with staged compliance dates for substances and mixtures and a transition period allowing compliance with either this section or the previous §1910.1200 revised as of July 1, 2023.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substances: manufacturers/importers/distributors must comply no later than January 19, 2026; employers update alternative workplace labeling/hazard communication program and provide training for newly identified hazards no later than July 20, 2026. Mixtures: manufacturers/importers/distributors must comply no later than July 19, 2027; employers update labeling/program/training no later than January 19, 2028. Between May 20, 2024 and these dates, parties may comply with either this section or the prior revision, or both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hazard classification principle — intrinsic properties and three-step process
rubrics_metrics.description: Hazard classification considers only the intrinsic hazardous properties of chemicals and incorporates three steps: (a) identification of relevant data regarding hazards; (b) review of those data to ascertain hazards; (c) determination whether the chemical will be classified as hazardous and the degree of hazard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification is based on intrinsic properties. Expert judgment is required for many hazard classes. Consider impurities, additives or constituents if they exceed cut-off/concentration limits for a hazard class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Available data, test methods, and data quality
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no requirement for testing chemicals; the criteria for determining health hazards are test-method neutral (do not specify particular test methods) provided methods are scientifically validated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientifically validated methods are those whose reliability and relevance are established. Any test conducted according to recognized scientific principles may be used. Test conditions should be standardized for reproducibility. Existing test data are acceptable. Consider biological availability — a chemical need not be classified if conclusive experimental data show it is not biologically available. Epidemiological and human experience data shall be taken into account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification based on weight of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When criteria are not directly satisfied by data, classification shall be determined on the basis of the total weight of evidence using expert judgment, considering all available information (in vitro, animal data, human experience, case reports).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate quality and consistency of data. Reliable human data generally have precedence, but well-conducted animal studies can justify classification when human data are lacking. Consider route of exposure, mechanistic and metabolism studies to determine human relevance; if mechanism not relevant to humans, do not classify. A single strong positive study may justify classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture classification sequence and exception for certain hazards
rubrics_metrics.description: Process for classification of mixtures: (a) use test data for the complete mixture when available; (b) when mixture data unavailable, apply bridging principles in each health hazard chapter; (c) if bridging principles cannot be applied, use methods described in each chapter for estimating hazards based on known information (e.g., cut-off/concentration limits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: For Carcinogenicity, Germ Cell Mutagenicity, and Reproductive Toxicity, mixtures shall be classified based upon information on ingredient substances unless case-by-case justification is provided for classifying based on the mixture as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cut-off values / concentration limits for untested mixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: When classifying an untested mixture based on ingredient hazards, cut-off values/concentration limits for classified ingredients are used for several hazard classes, but the classifier must consider whether hazard may be evident below the cut-off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If classifier has information that ingredient hazard is evident below the specified cut-off, classify accordingly. In exceptional cases, conclusive data may show hazard will not be evident above the cut-off and mixture may be classified accordingly, provided data exclude possibility that ingredient behaves differently in the mixture and mixture doesn't contain ingredients that would affect that determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of synergistic or antagonistic effects in mixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluators must take into account all available information about potential synergistic effects among ingredients of a mixture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lowering classification on the basis of antagonistic effects may be done only if the determination is supported by sufficient data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridging principles for classifying untested mixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a mixture has not been tested but sufficient data on ingredients and similar mixtures exist, use bridging principles to characterize hazards: Dilution, Batching, Concentration of mixtures, Interpolation within one hazard category, Substantially similar mixtures, and Aerosols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These principles ensure available data are used to the greatest extent for hazard characterization; specific application rules are provided for each principle (see separate bridging-principle entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridging principle — Dilution
rubrics_metrics.description: If a tested mixture is diluted with a diluent having equivalent or lower toxicity classification than the least toxic original ingredient and which is not expected to affect toxicity, then the diluted mixture shall be classified as equivalent to the original tested mixture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For Acute Toxicity classification, the additivity formula (A.1.3.6.1) may also apply where specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridging principle — Batching
rubrics_metrics.description: Toxicity of a tested production batch of a mixture can be assumed substantially equivalent to another untested production batch of the same mixture when produced by or under control of the same chemical manufacturer, unless there is reason to believe significant variation exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If significant variation is likely such that toxicity may have changed, a new classification is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridging principle — Concentration of mixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: If a tested mixture classified in Category 1 has the concentration of ingredients in Category 1 increased, the resulting untested mixture shall be classified in Category 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to specified hazard classes (A.1, A.2, A.3, A.4, A.8, A.9, A.10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridging principle — Interpolation within one hazard category
rubrics_metrics.description: For three mixtures with identical ingredients where two tested mixtures A and B are in the same hazard category and an untested mixture C has ingredient concentrations intermediate to A and B, mixture C is assumed to be in the same hazard category as A and B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies for mixtures classified under relevant hazard chapters (A.1–A.10 where specified).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridging principle — Substantially similar mixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two mixtures A+B and C+B where concentration of B is essentially the same and concentration of A equals C, and data on toxicity for A and C are substantially equivalent, if one mixture is classified based on test data, the other can be assigned the same hazard category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires A and C to be substantially equivalent and not expected to affect toxicity of B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridging principle — Aerosols
rubrics_metrics.description: An aerosol form of a mixture shall be classified in the same hazard category as the tested non-aerosolized form of the mixture, provided the added propellant does not affect the toxicity when spraying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies for specified hazard classes (A.1, A.2, A.3, A.4, A.8, A.9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acute toxicity — definition and numeric classification criteria (Table A.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acute toxicity refers to serious adverse health effects (lethality) after single or short-term oral, dermal, or inhalation exposure. Substances are allocated to four hazard categories based on acute toxicity by route according to numeric cut-off criteria expressed as LD50/LC50 or ATE values (see Table A.1.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table A.1.1 provides ATE cutoffs for oral, dermal, inhalation (gases, vapors, dusts/mists) for Categories 1–4 (e.g., Oral Category 1: ATE ≤ 5 mg/kg; Category 2: >5 ≤ 50; Category 3: >50 ≤ 300; Category 4: >300 ≤ 2000). Inhalation cut-offs are based on 4-hour testing exposures; conversions from 1-hour data are specified (divide by 2 for gases/vapors, 4 for dusts/mists). Definitions: dust, mist, vapor are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred test species and selection of LD50/LC50 values
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred test species for acute toxicity: rat for oral and inhalation; rat or rabbit for dermal evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When experimental data are available for several species, scientific judgment should be used to select the most appropriate LD50 value. Existing test data generated under existing systems should be accepted when reclassifying. Human experience data should be considered in a weight-of-evidence approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respiratory tract corrosivity evaluation and labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: If data indicate the mechanism of toxicity was corrosivity and the classifier determines the chemical is corrosive to the respiratory tract, the classifier must consider corrosivity to the respiratory tract and label accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If corrosive to respiratory tract and effect leads to lethality, include acute toxicity pictogram, hazard statement, and the hazard statement 'corrosive to the respiratory tract' and corrosive pictogram. If corrosive but not lethal, address under Specific Target Organ Toxicity (STOT) hazard classes. If data insufficient for STOT but skin or eye data indicate possible respiratory corrosivity, use skin/eye data for classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of mixtures for acute toxicity — tiered approach and relevant ingredients
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of mixtures for acute toxicity is tiered and depends on available information: (a) if mixture test data available, classify on mixture data; (b) if not, use bridging principles; (c) if those not applicable, use ingredient-based estimation methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification may be carried out for each route, but only required for one route if that route is followed for all ingredients and no evidence suggests multiple-route toxicity. Use the most severe hazard category for pictogram/signal word. 'Relevant ingredients' are those present at ≥1% (w/w for solids/liquids/dusts/mists/vapors and v/v for gases); consider ingredients <1% if they may affect classification (notably Category 1 or 2 ingredients). When a classified mixture is used as an ingredient, its ATE (actual or derived) is used in calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additivity formula and handling unknown-ingredient toxicity in mixtures (A.1.3.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: When data are available for all ingredients, the ATE of the mixture is calculated from ATE values for all relevant ingredients using the additivity formula; for ingredients without ATEs, derived conversion values or conservative approaches are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an ingredient with unknown acute toxicity is present ≥1% and the mixture is untested, the mixture cannot be given a definitive ATE; the label and SDS must state the percent of the mixture consisting of ingredient(s) of unknown acute toxicity. If total concentration of relevant unknown-toxicity ingredients is ≤10%, the additivity formula is adjusted (detailed in A.1.3.6.2.4). Table A.1.2 provides conversion from category/range to point estimates for oral/dermal/gases/vapors/dusts/mists (e.g., Oral Category 2 -> 5 mg/kg point estimate; Dermal Category 3 -> 300 mg/kg, etc.). Use a highly trained expert for estimating when data are incomplete; if insufficient information to estimate reliably, follow provisions for unknowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skin corrosion vs irritation definitions and classification tiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Skin corrosion refers to irreversible skin damage (visible necrosis through epidermis into dermis). Skin irritation refers to reversible skin damage after initial exposure. Substances are allocated to Category 1 (corrosion, with possible subcategories 1A–1C) or Category 2 (irritation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify based on all available and relevant information; use internationally validated methods where possible (e.g., OECD TG). A tiered approach organizes information into levels for decision-making; when information within a tier is inconsistent, use weight-of-evidence within that tier. Existing reliable human data should be given high weight for classification (occupational, consumer, transport, emergency, epidemiological, clinical reports).
